claims.text: As-cast/annealed HfNbTaTiZr has significant microstructural heterogeneity and locally distorted lattice regions.
Refined annealing and thermomechanical processing will minimize microstructural heterogeneity and reduce local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortions and microstructural heterogeneities modify dislocation nucleation and lattice stability.
Local distortions in the as-cast state reduce the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation.
A reduced dislocation-nucleation barrier causes an earlier onset of elastic instability.
Elastic instability can manifest as elastic strain-induced amorphization.
Local atomic inhomogeneity is associated with the onset of elastic strain-induced amorphization in high-entropy alloys.
Elastic strain-induced amorphization occurs when local elastic strain approaches approximately 10%.
Local distortions promote greater changes in atomic spacing during heating.
Greater heating-induced atomic-spacing changes increase the thermal expansion coefficient.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr will have a lower elastic strain threshold than homogenized HfNbTaTiZr.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr will exhibit elastic instability earlier than homogenized HfNbTaTiZr.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr will have a higher thermal expansion coefficient than homogenized HfNbTaTiZr.
As-cast and homogenized HfNbTaTiZr will exhibit different elastic moduli detectable by in situ diffraction.
The proposed mechanism should remain applicable from approximately 298 K to 1223 K.
In situ diffraction can reliably capture lattice-strain evolution up to approximately 10% elastic strain.
Quantitative thermal-expansion differences and precise elastic-threshold values remain uncertain and require experimental calibration.

The hypothesis is falsified if, under matched conditions, the as-cast samples show neither a statistically significant lower elastic strain threshold nor a higher thermal expansion coefficient than the homogenized samples.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says local distortions reduce the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation, whereas both cited records attribute amorphization to depressed dislocation nucleation or inhibition of defect-mediated plasticity. The direction of the claimed dislocation effect is opposite to the cited mechanism.
